div.div: The native WebSocket method works, until the engagement needs a conversation or OAuth 2.0. Moving the socket into a service of your own buys back both, and the platform never knows the difference.

div.span:
Every turn arrives on a
brand new connection, so
nothing is remembered.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 538px; height: 1px; padding-top: 131px; margin-left: 823px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #333333;
display: inline-block; font-size: 11px; font-family: Helvetica; color: #333333; line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div:
What that costs you
• No stateful multi-turn. Attack sequences run as independent prompts. The
chained attacks that need a conversation to build on cannot run at all.
• No OAuth 2.0. Headers and Basic only. An agent behind an OAuth 2.0 token
endpoint is out of reach on this method whatever else you configure.
• A private WebSocket target also needs channel client v1.3.0 or higher.

turn 1 POST, session_id in the body
turn 2 POST, same session_id
turn 3 POST, same session_id
Stateless from the platform's point of view.
Each POST is complete on its own.

div.span:
• Holds one persistent WebSocket per session
• Keeps the conversation history behind the session id
• Exchanges and refreshes the OAuth 2.0 token before
each frame it sends
• Reassembles streamed chunks into one reply

One connection, held open
across every turn, so the
agent's own session state
accumulates the way a real
conversation would.

div.b: Session state has to live somewhere that survives a restart

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 1348px; height: 1px; padding-top: 811px; margin-left: 19px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #333333;

div.div:
A dictionary in the wrapper process is the obvious first implementation and it works until the process restarts. An Attack Library scan runs for about five hours; a container
recycled in the middle of one drops every in-flight conversation, and the attacks that depended on earlier turns quietly stop making sense rather than failing loudly.
For a short scan that is a reasonable trade. For a long agent-led run, back the session map with Redis or a table keyed on the session id, and make the wrapper reconnect
the socket rather than lose the conversation.
